classification_signals: The article is titled 'Book Reviews' and specifically reviews 'The Perception of Color' by Ralph M. Evans.
The text uses phrases like 'In this book, Evans undertakes...', 'Evans introduces and defines...', 'The only criticism I might make...'
The author of the review is Peter K. Kaiser, distinct from the author of the book being reviewed.
title: The Perception of Color

findings.antecedent: Evans's proposed variables for color description (hue, saturation, brightness, lightness, brilliance)
findings.consequent: Description of colors
findings.quote: He defines, marshals evidence for, and uses five variables by which colors should be described, thus adding two to the classic three: hue, saturation, and brightness. His contribution is the addition of "lightness" and "brilliance."

findings.antecedent: Presence of more than one stimulus, perceived differences, surround constancy, chromaticity/sensitivity changes
findings.consequent: Dimensionality of color perception (5, 4, or 3 dimensions) and dependence of lightness/brilliance
findings.quote: ...in the presence of more than one stimulus we are always dealing with systems that are potentially five dimensional as far as appearance is concerned, but the number of potential dimensions is reduced to four if we restrict ourselves to perceived differences, and to three only if the surround for a given stimulus is constant and controls the sensitivity state of the eye.

findings.consequent: Difficulty for novice readers interested in color perception
findings.quote: This would be a difficult book for the novice interested in color perception.

findings.antecedent: Reading traditional texts (referred to by Evans) prior to Evans's book
findings.consequent: Better understanding of Evans's book for novices
findings.quote: The novice would do well to read some of the tradi- tional texts to which Evans refers, prior to tackling this book.

findings.consequent: Valuable reading for experts in color vision
findings.quote: The Perception of Color is valuable reading for the expert in color vision who may wish to broaden his perspective.

findings.consequent: Adequacy for handling color perception
findings.quote: Evans shows, clearly, that colorimetry is a limited science and cannot adequately handle color perception.

findings.antecedent: Simultaneous learning of colorimetry and Evans's approach from the book
findings.consequent: Difficulty for novices
findings.quote: The novice may find the dual tasks of learning colorimetry and the Evans approach to color perception difficult to achieve in this tightly written book.

findings.antecedent: Lack of a unified glossary in Evans's book
findings.consequent: Reduced usefulness/clarity for readers
findings.quote: Unfortunately, Evans provides only a partial glossary on page 96 of the terms and concepts that he introduces. A unified glossary of all terms and concepts, at the end of the book, would have been useful.

findings.antecedent: Blurring of Evans's personal opinion and interpretation of literature in the book
findings.consequent: Difficulty for reviewer to distinguish between them
findings.quote: I sometimes found it difficult to dis- tinguish between Evans's personal opinion of how colored objects are perceived and his interpretation of information from the liter- ature.

findings.consequent: Reflection of Evans's biases rather than perception of an average observer
findings.quote: Some de- scriptions may represent Evans's biases more than the perception we would expect of an average observer.

findings.consequent: Not equally bright (observation leading to 'brilliance' variable)
findings.quote: One of the reasons why Evans introduces the variable "bril- liance" is the observation that colored stimuli that are equal in luminance are usually not equally bright.

findings.antecedent: Methodological differences (direct heterochromatic brightness matching vs. flicker photometry)
findings.consequent: Discrepancy between brightness and luminance
findings.quote: A number of investigators during the last ten years have studied this discrepancy and come to the conclusion that the basic difference between brightness and luminance rests in the different methodologies underlying these measures.

findings.consequent: Accounting for the relationship between brightness/luminance methods and visual physiology
findings.quote: The relationship be- tween these methods and visual physiology seems relatively well ac- counted for by current color-vision theory.

findings.antecedent: More-saturated spectral lights vs. less-saturated lights (all adjusted to equal luminance)
findings.consequent: More-saturated lights perceived as brighter (reviewer's personal observation)
findings.quote: In my own color lexicon, I see the more-saturated spectral lights as brighter than less-saturated lights when all are adjusted to equal luminance.

findings.antecedent: Stimuli equated for luminance during flicker photometry
findings.consequent: Equated for achromatic activity (reviewer's assumption)
findings.quote: When various stimuli are equated for luminance, I assume they are equated for achromatic activity because, during flicker photometry, only the achromatic part of the visual system enters into the minimum-flicker judgment.

findings.consequent: Perception of brightness associated with both achromatic and chromatic visual activity (reviewer's model)
findings.quote: But when stimuli are not being flickered, we perceive the brightness associ- ated with the achromatic visual activity and also the chromatic vis- ual activity.

findings.consequent: Conveys hue and brightness information (reviewer's model)
findings.quote: The chromatic visual activity conveys hue and bright- ness information, whereas the achromatic visual system carries brightness and whiteness information.

findings.consequent: Carries brightness and whiteness information (reviewer's model)
findings.quote: The chromatic visual activity conveys hue and bright- ness information, whereas the achromatic visual system carries brightness and whiteness information.

findings.consequent: Basis for introducing two additional variables (lightness, brilliance)
findings.quote: First, they form the basis from which Evans introduces his two additional variables.

findings.consequent: Similarity to functions derived in other ways (e.g., saturation-discrimination curves, equivalent contrast curves, brightness-matching luminous-efficiency ratio, white content estimates)
findings.quote: Second, the shapes of these curves are similar to functions that may be derived in other ways. As Evans noted, G_o functions are similar to satura- tion-discrimination curves.

findings.consequent: Tapping the same visual processes as other experimental procedures
findings.quote: Probably Evans's G_o functions tap the same visual processes that are effective in the other experimental procedures.

findings.consequent: No achromatic component perceived (Evans's statement)
findings.quote: Evans makes the astounding statement that-"...aside perhaps from yellow, no achromatic component at all is usually perceived in a pure spectrum." (page 120).

findings.consequent: Different amounts of achromatic content reported (Jacobs's finding)
findings.quote: Jacobs found that different amounts of achromatic content were reported as a function of wavelength.

findings.consequent: Resemblance to saturation and G_o functions
findings.quote: As mentioned previously, the shape of Jacobs's curves resemble saturation and G_o functions.

findings.antecedent: Monochromatic stimuli differing in chromatic strength/brilliance
findings.consequent: Accordance with what is actually seen (Evans's assertion)
findings.quote: Evans asserts that "to assume instead that the various mono- chromatic stimuli differ in chromatic strength, that is, brilliance, accords far more nearly with what is actually seen." (page 120).

findings.antecedent: Evans's view (no achromatic response to spectral stimuli other than yellow) vs. Jacobs's observers estimating whiteness in spectral colors
findings.consequent: Inconsistency/difficulty in reconciliation (reviewer's critique)
findings.quote: I don't understand how Evans would reconcile his view of color perception, which assumes no achromatic response to spectral stim- uli other than yellow, with the ability of Jacobs's observers to estimate the amounts of whiteness in spectral colors.

findings.consequent: Color vision mediated by cones and rods (proposed mechanism)
findings.quote: He suggested to Selig Hecht the possibility that color vision is mediated by cones and rods.

findings.antecedent: Speculations (e.g., rod/cone mediation of color vision)
findings.consequent: Not suitable for a published book (Hecht's opinion, quoted by Evans)
findings.quote: ...while such speculations may prompt very interesting dinner conversation they have no place in a published book.

findings.consequent: Adequate data on color perception (proposed as the only way)
findings.quote: Evans repeatedly suggests the use of "inter-eye comparisons," suggesting that that is the only way that adequate data on color perception can be obtained.

findings.antecedent: Color-naming methods (proved useful in past ten years)
findings.consequent: Could have been used for Evans's suggested inter-eye studies
findings.quote: I found that some of the inter-eye studies suggested by Evans could be or have been done by color- naming methods that have been proved useful during the past ten years.

findings.consequent: Well-written
findings.quote: This is a well-written book.

findings.antecedent: Sparse use of graphical and other illustrative aids in Evans's book
findings.consequent: Reduced clarity/effectiveness in description of ideas
findings.quote: The only criticism I might make, in addition to the lack of a unified glossary, is the rather sparse use of graphical and other illustrative aids in the description of ideas.

limitations: The book lacks a unified glossary of terms and concepts.
It was difficult for the reviewer to distinguish between Evans's personal opinion and his interpretation of literature.
Some descriptions in the book may represent Evans's biases more than the perception of an average observer.
The book makes sparse use of graphical and other illustrative aids in the description of ideas.
minimum_safe_summary: The paper is a review of Ralph M. Evans's book 'The Perception of Color,' which proposes a five-dimensional system for describing color perception, adding 'lightness' and 'brilliance' to the classic three. The reviewer finds the book valuable for experts but challenging for novices due to its density and lack of a comprehensive glossary. Key findings include Evans's argument that colorimetry is limited for color perception, his G_o curves as a basis for new variables, and the reviewer's critique regarding the distinction between Evans's personal opinions and literature interpretation, as well as the book's sparse use of illustrative aids. A limitation noted is the potential for Evans's descriptions to reflect personal biases rather than average observer perception.
